title: Dēpology Design System
subtitle: Turning mobile commerce friction into reusable navigation, buybox, cart, checkout, and responsive product-page patterns.
problem: Depology was preparing new skincare launches for paid social testing, but mobile conversion was leaking at two repeat decision points: the buybox and header navigation. Heatmaps and analytics showed shoppers hesitating where they should have been comparing, choosing, and checking out.
solution: The redesign focused on those two friction points. I simplified the mobile buybox, clarified CTA hierarchy, and reduced navigation noise, then validated the changes through A/B testing before the patterns were adopted across new product pages.
body: Depology was at an inflection point. The Korean skincare brand had built a devoted following on Instagram and was ready to scale through aggressive product launches and paid advertising. But there was a problem: their existing product pages weren't converting at the rates needed to justify increased ad spend. With multiple new products queued for shadow testing—a strategy where products are launched quietly to gauge market response before full rollout—the team needed landing pages that could turn Instagram traffic into customers efficiently.

The first step was diagnosis. Heatmap analysis revealed that mobile users were tapping repeatedly on elements within the product buybox, suggesting confusion about how to add items to cart or select variants. Conversion funnel data confirmed the suspicion: a significant percentage of users were abandoning their sessions at the product page stage. Session length metrics told another story—users who did engage were spending less time on site than expected, often bouncing after encountering the cluttered header navigation. These weren't assumptions; they were patterns backed by behavioral data.

Armed with these insights, the redesign focused on surgical improvements rather than wholesale changes. The mobile buybox was reimagined with a clearer visual hierarchy: variant selectors were made more prominent, the add-to-cart button was enlarged and repositioned for thumb-friendly access, and product information was reorganized to answer questions in the order customers naturally asked them. The header navigation was simplified dramatically, reducing menu options and improving the information architecture to help users find what they needed without overwhelming them. Every decision was testable, measurable, and directly tied to observed user behavior.

The validation process was methodical. Test runs were launched on select product pages, with conversion rates monitored daily. The results were striking: the new designs drove a conversion rate increase that validated every hypothesis. With data in hand, the pitch to product and marketing leadership was straightforward—these changes weren't subjective design preferences, they were proven performance improvements. The stakeholders backed the rollout, and the new UI was implemented first across all new product landing pages, then gradually adopted across the entire site. Depology's mobile experience had transformed from a conversion bottleneck into a growth engine.

title: Explainable Property Search
subtitle: A technical UX case study translating ambiguous renter language into editable intent, ranked recommendations, and inspectable Python + JSON search logic.
problem: Property seekers often describe intent in natural language, but standard filters split that intent across separate controls and leave users unsure whether the system understood their requirements.
solution: A mobile-first NLP search flow that turns renter language into editable chips, runs against a Python-backed ranking layer and structured JSON property data, then explains matches in the interface.

title: Worldschooling
subtitle: A launch-ready education-travel platform that narrowed a large booking vision into programme comparison, eligibility checks, and deposit confidence.
problem: I read Worldschooling as a release-scope problem, not a cosmetic website brief. The team wanted a full education-travel platform, but the first launch needed to help parents compare programmes, judge fit, and understand the deposit step without waiting for a custom booking system.
solution: The first release became a decision path: programme discovery, tier comparison, detail pages, eligibility form, and a universal deposit link. It kept the important customer choices visible while removing months of platform scope.
body: The website brief needed to be separated from the real product constraint. The planned platform had enough pieces to become a long product build: campus pages, subject pages, programme pages, search, blog, booking portal, and payment. For an early-stage education-travel business, that would have delayed the thing the team needed most: a credible surface that could explain programmes and support conversations with parents, students, and stakeholders.

Looking at the journey from the parent side changed the brief. A parent does not start by asking whether the site has a custom booking engine. They ask what the programme is, whether it fits their child, what is included, what the commitment is, and what happens after they submit details. That made the booking portal less important than comparison, eligibility, and deposit clarity.

The first-release booking engine became a simpler path: homepage, programme filtering, detail pages, eligibility form, and a universal deposit payment link. The tradeoff was clear. The flow was less automated for the business, but it made the product launchable and kept the important decision points visible to customers.

The homepage exposed programme categories instead of burying the range behind static cards. The selector gave users a way to move between themes and levels, while the detail pages carried the specific confidence cues: what the programme includes, who it is for, and what the next step requires. Recommendation cards on entry-level pages introduced higher-value options where comparison already made sense.

Launch readiness is the safest claim here, not proven conversion. The new structure gave the team a usable sales and fundraising surface without waiting for a full booking platform. If I continued the work, the live funnel would be the next thing to inspect: which programme categories people open, where parents leave the eligibility form, and whether recommendation cards lead to deposit clicks or just extra browsing.

The homepage category selector gives mid-tier programmes a clear entry point before users are deep in the site, making comparison part of the first screen logic.
Recommendation cards on entry-level programme pages show the next tier when users are already comparing dates, themes, and value.
Programme cards were written and structured around parent/student comparison: what the trip is, who it suits, and what commitment comes next.
Physical brand materials helped the digital platform feel connected to the real student travel experience, not just the sales page.
The visual system gave the team reusable rules for programme pages, campaign assets, and student-facing materials.

title: Worldover.io
subtitle: A compliance command-centre case study turning threshold risk, entity scope, production evidence, alerts, and report blockers into one scannable decision workflow.
problem: Compliance teams move between different mindspaces: risk triage, production review, alert setup, report readiness, and evidence audit. The earlier dashboard showed plenty of data, but blurred the action needed to clear a threshold breach.
solution: I redesigned the experience around a multi-tab command flow. Each tab protects a separate mental mode, while Risk Command narrows the main task to detect, decide, and assign using entity-specific dummy data.

content.value: Worldover sits in a high-consequence compliance space where users need confidence before acting. A single annual threshold breach can involve production plans, legal entity scope, registration limits, stale data, plant owners, evidence imports, and report-generation blockers. The product challenge was not simply showing more information. It was helping a user know which kind of work they were doing at any moment.

content.title: Why the live demo looks different from the original delivery
content.value: The embedded Risk Command Centre is a recent April 2026 update of the earlier Worldover delivery. The original work established the compliance dashboard direction and visual system; this newer demo revisits the same product problem with a more operational lens. I kept the domain, compliance logic, and Worldover brand cues, but rebuilt the experience to show how the product could move from monitoring data to resolving threshold risk. That is why the live demo intentionally looks and behaves differently from the older dashboard screens.

content.title: Risk Command Centre
content.description: Change the entity selector to see the backend display conditions switch across the whole interface: case status, production facts, alerts, reporting blockers, evidence, and readiness all update from the dummy data model.

content.kicker: What improved from the old delivery
content.title: Five design upgrades in the April 2026 demo

items.title: From passive dashboard to action command centre
items.value: The older delivery focused on surfacing compliance data. The updated demo turns the same risk context into a guided workflow: detect the signal, decide the mitigation, assign the next owner, and watch readiness change.

items.title: Clearer mindspace separation
items.value: Risk Command, Production, Alerts, Reporting, and Evidence now live in separate tabs. This preserves context for different user tasks instead of mixing tables, charts, rules, and audit records into one overloaded screen.

items.title: Entity-aware data behavior
items.value: The prototype is backed by structured dummy data with entity-specific display conditions. Switching from group view to Germany, France, or UK changes severity, metrics, readiness, production facts, alerts, reporting blockers, evidence, and the resolution drawer.

items.title: Sharper compliance storytelling
items.value: The case now communicates not just what is above threshold, but why it matters, what is blocking closure, who owns the next action, and what evidence is still missing before reporting can proceed.

items.title: More polished production-facing interaction design
items.value: The April 2026 demo applies a tighter Worldover-inspired visual language, better text hierarchy, resolved z-index/layout issues, accessible real threshold labels, and browser-tested responsive behavior.

content.value: The main UX decision was to keep multiple tabs rather than collapse everything into one mega-dashboard. Risk Command is for deciding what to do. Production is for factory contribution and threshold consumption. Alerts are for rules and escalation. Reporting is for blockers and draft gates. Evidence is for imports and audit trail. I kept that separation because each tab protects a different kind of attention.

Inside Risk Command, the flow is intentionally narrow: detect the signal, decide the mitigation, then assign the work. This reduces the cognitive load for a compliance operator who may be under deadline pressure. The UI still exposes supporting data, but it does not ask the user to interpret every table before taking the next step.

content.caption: The case study reframes Worldover from a static compliance dashboard into an operational command centre with clearer mode separation.

content.value: To make the prototype realistic, I mapped a dummy backend payload that covers the display states the interface needs: severity classes, readiness rules, chemical records, entity views, production charts, alert rules, reporting sections, evidence records, drawer actions, and empty states. Entity selection is no longer a label-only filter; it changes the full display context.

title: Travel to Qin
subtitle: A trust-building travel site for international visitors who needed itinerary clarity before enquiring about China trips.
problem: Travel to Qin was a trust problem, not just a travel-site refresh. The old Shopify page could take payment, but it did not answer what foreign visitors needed before enquiring: who runs the trip, what is included, how support works, and why the agency is credible.
solution: I rebuilt the page around proof before purchase: a video-led opening, destination context, itinerary detail, service explanation, and a clearer enquiry path. A CMS made the content easier to update as trips and campaigns changed.
body: The original site problem was trust order, not visual polish. The page behaved like a checkout before the visitor had enough reasons to trust the trip. A foreign traveller considering China needs context before commitment: what they will see, who will guide them, how the itinerary is organised, what support exists, and why this agency is credible.

The site was treated as a trust sequence. The first screen needed to make the destination feel real, but the rest of the page needed to answer practical questions. Beautiful imagery could create interest, but it could not carry the whole job. The content order had to move visitors from inspiration to understanding to enquiry.

Proof came before purchase. A video-led opening established place and scale, then the page moved into itinerary structure, destination context, service explanation, and next-step clarity. That gave the visitor a reason to keep reading instead of landing directly on a transaction page with too many unanswered questions.

The same logic carried into the brand work. Chinese calligraphy and landscape references gave the identity cultural grounding, while the colour palette, typography, cards, and layout system made the information easier to scan. The site needed to feel connected to China without turning into a poster. The brand had to support the service, not sit on top of it.

The move from Shopify to a CMS was practical, not just technical. Travel content changes: itineraries, seasonal campaigns, stories, and destination highlights all need editing. A CMS gave the team a way to keep the site current without rebuilding the page for every campaign.

A stronger trust and sales surface is the right claim, not automatic conversion uplift. The work gave stakeholders a site that could support social traffic, brochures, and future app surfaces with one visual language. If I continued the work, I would inspect where visitors pause, which itinerary sections they read, which social channels send qualified enquiries, and what questions still appear before someone contacts the team.

images.caption: The redesign moved the site from transaction-first checkout to a trust-building travel surface with destination context, itinerary detail, and enquiry clarity.
The page structure answers pre-enquiry questions in order: what the trip feels like, what is included, why the agency is credible, and what to do next.
Itinerary content was treated as proof, not decoration. The brochure format helps visitors understand the trip before speaking to the team.
The identity uses Chinese visual references while keeping the system practical enough for service information, campaigns, and future product surfaces.
Destination cards break the travel offer into scannable choices so visitors can compare places before enquiring.
The print system extends the same trust sequence into offline sales material: context first, itinerary proof second, enquiry path last.

title: TUTU FUTURE
subtitle: a strategic rebrand for a Chinese study tour operator expanding beyond hiking trips into academic and cultural programs.
problem: TUTU FUTURE had outgrown its hiking-led study travel identity. The brand still felt warm, but it was too narrow for academic courses, art workshops, STEM activities, language immersion, and city-based cultural trips.
solution: I reframed exploration as physical, cultural, academic, and personal. The updated logo, bilingual lockup, colour system, programme treatments, and mascot gave the team more range without losing the brand's student-facing warmth.
body: TUTU FUTURE's problem was brand fit, not taste. The company had started with an outdoors-heavy study travel identity, but the offer had widened into academic courses, art programmes, STEM workshops, language learning, and city-based cultural experiences. The old green hiking world still had warmth, but it was beginning to tell only one part of the story.

I approached the rebrand as a positioning problem first. The useful idea was not to abandon exploration, but to widen it. Exploration could mean a mountain trail, a museum, a lab session, a language classroom, or a first independent trip abroad. That gave the identity a reason to move away from literal hiking symbols without losing the sense of curiosity that made the original brand approachable.

The logo, bilingual lockup, colour system, and mascot were designed to make different programme types feel related without making them look identical. Language, art, STEM, culture, and outdoor offers each needed enough visual distinction for social campaigns and brochures, but the system still had to feel like one company when parents and students compared options.

The most useful outcome was a brand system the team could keep using. It gave TUTU FUTURE a clearer way to package a broader study-travel portfolio, rather than forcing every new programme back into the same outdoors image. If the work continued, I would inspect which programme visuals help students recognise fit fastest, and whether parents understand the widened offer without needing a sales explanation.

A flexible color system that allows each program type—language, art, STEM, outdoor—to have its own visual personality while maintaining brand cohesion across all touchpoints.

The brand identity system deployed across print and digital touchpoints, demonstrating scalability and versatility for social media campaigns, promotional materials, and student-facing communications.

title: Stair Aid
subtitle: an assistive mobility device that enables faster, safer stair navigation for people with temporary lower-limb injuries.
problem: Standard crutches work for flat ground, but stairs require different support positions. Manual length adjustment is slow and awkward, leaving injured users to choose between the wrong crutch length, pausing mid-stair, or moving with less stability.
solution: I focused StairAid on fast stair adjustment. A one-handed trigger changes crutch length in seconds, supporting a front-back stance on stairs and a matched stance on level ground, with the curved tip and forearm brace serving the same transition goal.
body: The first observation was simple: stairs change the job of a crutch. On flat ground, matching lengths make sense. On stairs, the user needs a diagonal stance, with one support higher and one lower, so the body can move through a safer tripod-like position. Standard crutches ask users to choose between moving awkwardly or stopping to adjust length by hand.

The early tests made the design problem narrower. Uneven crutch lengths reduced stair descent time from 8 seconds to 6 seconds in the observed trial, but the manual adjustment process was still too slow for real use. I treated the mechanism as the core experience: if the crutch could not change length quickly and confidently, the stair gait insight would not matter.

The mechanism moved through several iterations. An external locking system made the idea visible but added complexity and made the product feel less resolved. Moving the mechanism inside the tube protected the form and reduced the number of exposed parts. The final principle used a lever, bike cable, wedge, and spring so a trigger pull could release length while the default state stayed locked.

The surrounding details followed the same stair-use logic. The curved tip gives a more useful contact point during angled movement and adjustment. The forearm brace supports more active weight shifts than an armpit crutch. Material choices were considered around load, weight, and manufacturability rather than appearance alone.

The strongest outcome is a validated product direction, not a finished medical device. The work shows that faster length adjustment can make stair movement feel more plausible and less disruptive. If the project continued, I would inspect longer-term comfort, repeated locking reliability, wet-step behaviour, and whether users understand the stair mode without coaching.

images.caption: Research indicated that the primary cause of chronic ankle instability was the failure of standard crutches to handle stairs safely, leading to the objective of designing a fast, safe, and comfortable stair-navigating mobility aid.

The core innovation relies on uneven crutch lengths, enabling users to adopt a stable front-back stance on stairs. This specific gait ensures 3/4 of the body weight is supported, preventing recurrent injury.
The Stairaid design allows users to seamlessly transition between level ground and stair modes by adjusting and locking the crutch length in just 3 seconds per piece using a quick-release trigger.
The internal locking mechanism utilizes a lever, bike cable, and wedge system to translate vertical hand motion into a horizontal locking pin action, providing secure and rapid length adjustment.
